Guides

What first foods are really for

In the second half of the first year, food is there for iron, energy, and learning to eat. It is not about hitting a protein percentage.

Findings

Iron is the first nutrient to run low. Healthy babies born at term have iron stores that last about six months. After that, milk alone can’t keep up.
Babies don’t need twice an adult’s share of protein. More protein in a baby’s diet is linked with faster weight gain, not better development.
Keep the fat in. Under two, full-fat dairy and a spoonful of oil are the right choice. Low-fat products are for older children and adults.
Fruit purée alone isn’t a meal plan. A plate needs an iron-rich food, a vegetable, and enough energy. Fruit is a welcome extra, not the meal.

Iron

By about six months, the iron stores built up before birth are running down just as your baby is growing fast. Breast milk is still valuable, but it has little iron. That’s why meat, lentils, beans, tofu, and iron-fortified cereal belong in the first weeks of solids, not after a long run of fruit and vegetables.

Vitamin C from fruit or vegetables at the same meal helps the body absorb iron from plants. Tea with meals does the opposite. A baby drinking enough infant formula already gets iron from it, but food still matters: it builds eating skills and the diet that follows the first year.

What about protein?

Adult diets are often described as about 12 to 15 percent protein by energy. Doubling that for a child would mean roughly a quarter of all calories from protein. That is not the infant target. Mature breast milk is closer to 5 to 8 percent protein by energy, and formula is deliberately kept in a modest range.

A randomised trial of infant formula found that more protein led to faster weight gain up to age two. Professional guidance takes this as a reason not to chase protein. Meat and pulses earn their place for iron, zinc, and texture, and because children learn to like them. Not for pushing the protein percentage up.

Fat and energy

The brain is still developing, and meals are small. A teaspoon of rapeseed or olive oil on a purée, or a little full-fat yogurt or pasteurised cheese, adds energy without salt. Low-fat milk and yogurt can wait until after the second birthday.

Flaxseed oil goes rancid quickly and shouldn’t be heated. You don’t need a pricey special oil blend. One ordinary oil, stirred in after cooking, is enough.

What goes on a good plate

A simple pattern that works: one iron-rich food, one vegetable, one familiar starch or fruit, and a little fat. Pumpkin, apple, pear, and banana are lovely but low in iron. Serve them alongside the iron food, not instead of it for weeks on end.

Across a varied week, plant proteins provide all the amino acids a baby needs. Not every meal has to include meat.
